title: Appeals Court Upholds Ruling Striking Down Trump's $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee
excerpt: The First Circuit denied the Trump administration's bid to reinstate the fee while its appeal proceeds, leaving USCIS barred from collecting the charge on new H-1B petitions.
body:
• The First Circuit Court of Appeals on July 24 denied the Trump administration's motion to stay a lower court ruling that struck down the $100,000 H-1B visa fee.
  • U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin ruled on June 8 that the fee constituted an unlawful tax that only Congress can impose, citing the Supreme Court's tariff ruling.
  • USCIS is now barred from collecting the $100,000 charge, though the merits appeal remains pending and could reverse the outcome.
  • Indian nationals, who receive roughly three-quarters of all H-1B approvals, stand to benefit most from the fee's removal.

A federal appeals court has rejected the Trump administration's attempt to reinstate a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas, leaving the controversial charge blocked nationwide while litigation over its legality continues.

The Boston-based First U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on July 24 declined to stay a lower court order that had struck down the fee, according to Reuters. The three-judge panel found the administration failed to demonstrate it was likely to succeed on appeal in showing it had not exceeded its authority.

How the Fee Was Imposed and Challenged

President Trump issued a proclamation on September 19, 2025, imposing the $100,000 supplemental payment on employers filing new H-1B petitions for foreign nationals outside the United States — those seeking consular processing or otherwise ineligible for a change or extension of existing H-1B status. The fee was layered on top of existing filing costs that typically ranged from $960 to $7,595.

A coalition of 20 Democratic state attorneys general filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, arguing the fee would devastate their ability to hire teachers, university faculty, researchers, and healthcare workers.

"The Court finds that the Policy imposes a tax on H-1B petitions without the requisite delegation by Congress."

— Judge Leo Sorokin, U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts

On June 8, 2026, Judge Leo Sorokin ruled the $100,000 payment was an unlawful tax. Drawing on the Supreme Court's ruling striking down Trump's emergency tariffs, Sorokin found the president had no authority under immigration law to levy a tax — a power reserved exclusively for Congress. The court also found the administration violated the Administrative Procedure Act by rolling out the policy without notice-and-comment rulemaking.

A Temporary Reprieve, Then a Firm Rejection

The administration moved quickly to preserve the fee. On June 12, Judge Sorokin granted a temporary administrative stay of his own order, allowing USCIS to continue collecting the $100,000 while the government sought emergency relief from the First Circuit. That pause kept the fee in place for roughly six weeks.

But the appeals court's July 24 decision ended that reprieve. The panel — composed of appointees of Democratic presidents — found the government had not met the standard for a stay, effectively restoring the district court's vacatur and barring USCIS from assessing or collecting the charge.

Conflicting Rulings Raise Supreme Court Prospect

The Massachusetts ruling stands in tension with a decision from a federal judge in Washington, D.C., who late last year rejected a challenge brought by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the Association of American Universities. That case is on appeal before the D.C. Circuit, which heard arguments in March. A separate challenge by religious groups and labor organizations is pending in San Francisco.

The split across federal courts raises the prospect that the issue could ultimately reach the Supreme Court.

Impact on Indian Workers

The H-1B program offers 65,000 visas annually, with an additional 20,000 for workers holding advanced degrees. Indian nationals receive roughly three-quarters of all H-1B approvals, making them the group most affected by the fee.

Few employers actually paid the charge. As of mid-February, USCIS had received just 85 payments of $100,000, according to court filings cited by Reuters. The fee's primary effect was to discourage H-1B petitions altogether, chilling international hiring at a time when technology firms, hospitals, and universities faced skilled-worker shortages.

"President Trump has clear legal authority to restrict entry of any class of aliens he determines is not in America's best interests, and that is exactly what he did."

— Taylor Rogers, White House spokeswoman

What Comes Next

The merits appeal remains pending before the First Circuit, and the D.C. Circuit could issue its own ruling at any time. Employers who shelved H-1B petitions can now file without the $100,000 charge, but immigration attorneys are cautioning against treating the decision as final — an appellate reversal could reinstate the fee without warning. The original proclamation was set to expire in September 2026, adding another layer of uncertainty.
